planting.note: Sow directly into loose, deep soil once the ground can be worked, and allow a long season for full-size roots since it bulks up more slowly than modern hybrid beets.

directions: Considered one of the oldest documented beet varieties still in cultivation, tracing back to at least the 1600s in France, where its name (French for toad) refers to the rough, dark gray-brown bark-like skin that develops as the root matures. Sow directly into loose, deep soil once the ground can be worked, and expect a slower bulking rate than modern hybrid beets, so allow a long season for full-size roots. The deep garnet flesh stays firm and sweet, making Crapaudine one of the best-keeping beets for winter root cellar storage. Light frost before harvest improves its already rich, earthy sweetness.

planting.note: Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil; harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops.

directions: An Italian heirloom documented in 19th-century European seed catalogs, grown for its flattened roots with distinctive pink-and-white concentric rings when sliced, milder and less earthy than solid red beets. It matures quickly, making it well suited to early spring sowings ahead of summer heat or a late-summer succession crop. Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil and harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops, which can also be cooked as greens.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; can be resown for a fall crop.

directions: One of the earliest American beet varieties on record, grown widely since the early 1800s and named for its flattened, turnip-like shape rather than any relation to actual turnips. It was the dominant garden beet in the United States for much of the 19th century before newer selections like Detroit Dark Red largely replaced it commercially. Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; the deep red roots have dense, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and pickling, and the plant can be resown for a fall crop as well.
sources: William Woys Weaver, Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

scientific_name: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa 'Purple Top Milan'

planting.note: Sow very early in spring before other crops are ready, or as a quick fall catch crop; pull roots promptly at 2-3 inches across.

directions: A traditional Italian heirloom prized for being one of the fastest turnips to reach the table, producing flattened white discs capped in bright purple-red in as little as five to six weeks. Its speed makes it ideal for very early spring sowing before other crops are ready, or for a quick fall catch crop after summer vegetables finish. The flesh is notably tender and mild when harvested young and small, becoming pithier if left to size up, so pull roots promptly at 2-3 inches across.

planting.note: Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor.

directions: A Central/Eastern European heirloom turnip grown historically in Poland and Russia for its round, golden-skinned roots with pale yellow flesh, a distinct look and flavor compared to the purple-top white types common in American gardens. It was traditionally valued for dual use as both a table vegetable and livestock forage. Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor and reduces the sharper bite common in summer-grown turnips.
